questions.question: A finite extensive-form game with perfect recall has no perfect Bayesian equilibrium in pure strategies. What can be concluded about its perfect Bayesian equilibria?
options: None exists, so play can only be predicted with Nash equilibrium
At least one exists, in mixed or behavioural strategies
One exists only if Bayes' rule is dropped on the path
One exists only if the game has perfect information

questions.question: In a perfect Bayesian equilibrium, at which information sets must each player's strategy be optimal given the beliefs $\mu$ and the other players' strategies?
options: At every information set, whether or not equilibrium play reaches it
Only at information sets reached with positive probability
Only at the initial node, when the whole strategy is planned
Only at singleton information sets, where beliefs are trivial

questions.question: In a perfect Bayesian equilibrium $(\sigma,\mu)$, how are the beliefs determined at an information set reached with positive probability under $\sigma$?
options: They may be any distribution the analyst finds plausible
By Bayes' rule from $\sigma$ and the common prior
They are equal to the prior, whatever the strategies
They are chosen to make the mover's action optimal

questions.question: In the (weak) perfect Bayesian equilibrium defined by sequential rationality, Bayes' rule on the path and free beliefs off it, what beliefs may be held at an information set reached with probability $0$?
options: Only the prior distribution over the nodes
Only beliefs that make the deviation unprofitable
Any probability distribution over its nodes
Only a degenerate belief putting probability $1$ on one node

questions.question: How is the set of strategy profiles of perfect Bayesian equilibria related to the set of Nash equilibria of the same extensive-form game?
options: Every PBE profile is a Nash equilibrium; not every Nash equilibrium is a PBE
Nash equilibria form the smaller set, contained in the PBE profiles
The two sets always coincide, since both require best responses
The two sets are unrelated, since PBE also needs beliefs

questions.question: An entrant chooses Out, giving (entrant, incumbent) payoffs $(0,3)$, or In; after In the incumbent chooses Accommodate $(2,1)$ or Fight $(-1,0)$. Which profile is a Nash equilibrium but not a perfect Bayesian equilibrium?
options: (In, Accommodate)
(In, Fight)
(Out, Accommodate)
(Out, Fight)

questions.question: An entrant of type $C$ (prior $p$) or $W$ picks Out (payoff $0$) or In; the incumbent sees only In and plays $A$ (accommodate) or $F$ (fight). Payoffs (entrant, incumbent): $C$: $A\,(2,1)$, $F\,(1,-1)$; $W$: $A\,(1,1)$, $F\,(-1,2)$. If the incumbent's belief after entry is $\mu=\mathbb{P}(C\mid\text{In})=\frac{1}{4}$, which action is sequentially rational for it?
options: Accommodate: Fight yields only $-\frac{1}{4}<1$
Fight, with expected payoff $\frac{5}{4}>1$
Fight: its payoff $\frac{1}{2}$ beats a passive $0$
Accommodate, as $C$ prefers being accommodated

questions.question: After entry, an incumbent who cannot see the entrant's type gets: against a competitive type, Fight $-2$ and Accommodate $1$; against a weak type, Fight $3$ and Accommodate $1$. For which beliefs $\mu$ in the competitive type is Fight sequentially rational?
options: $\mu\le\frac{1}{3}$
$\mu\ge\frac{2}{5}$
$\mu\le\frac{2}{5}$
$\mu\le\frac{1}{2}$

questions.question: An entrant of type $C$ (prior $p$) or $W$ picks Out (payoff $0$) or In; the incumbent sees only In and plays $A$ (accommodate) or $F$ (fight). Payoffs (entrant, incumbent): $C$: $A\,(2,1)$, $F\,(1,-1)$; $W$: $A\,(1,1)$, $F\,(-1,2)$. Let $p=0.6$ and consider a profile in which both types choose In. Which belief after entry must the incumbent hold in a perfect Bayesian equilibrium?
options: Any $\mu\in[0,1]$

questions.question: Player 1 chooses Out, ending with payoffs $(1,0)$, or In; after In, player 2 chooses Left $(0,2)$ or Right $(3,1)$, and every information set is a single node. What is the strategy profile of the perfect Bayesian equilibrium?
options: (Out, Left)
(In, Right)
(Out, Right)
(In, Left)

questions.question: Nature first draws an entrant's type, which the incumbent never observes, and the incumbent moves after the entrant. Why does subgame perfection fail to rule out non-credible threats here?
options: Subgame perfection requires knowing the type, which no player knows
Subgame perfection only applies to games with two players
Subgame perfection allows mixed strategies, which hide the threats
With no proper subgame, every Nash equilibrium is trivially subgame-perfect

questions.question: A perfect Bayesian equilibrium is supported by a pessimistic belief at an information set that equilibrium play never reaches. What must still be checked for the player who moves there?
options: Nothing, since unreached information sets do not affect payoffs
That the belief there was derived from the prior by Bayes' rule
That the belief there equals the belief on the equilibrium path
That the action there is optimal given the stated belief

questions.question: Why can a weak perfect Bayesian equilibrium (sequential rationality, Bayes' rule on the path, free beliefs off it) fail to be subgame-perfect in some games?
options: It does not require sequential rationality off the equilibrium path
It allows strictly dominated strategies on the equilibrium path
It puts no consistency requirement on beliefs inside an unreached subgame
It ignores the common prior when computing beliefs

questions.question: An entrant of type $C$ (prior $p$) or $W$ picks Out (payoff $0$) or In; the incumbent sees only In and plays $A$ (accommodate) or $F$ (fight). Payoffs (entrant, incumbent): $C$: $A\,(2,1)$, $F\,(1,-1)$; $W$: $A\,(1,1)$, $F\,(-1,2)$. Let $p=\frac{1}{5}$. Why is ‘both types enter and the incumbent accommodates’ not a perfect Bayesian equilibrium?
options: $\mu=\frac{1}{5}\le\frac{1}{3}$, so the incumbent must fight, and $W$ then prefers Out
$\mu$ off the path can be set high enough to justify accommodating
$C$ would rather stay out, since entering can be fought
Bayes' rule requires $\mu=1$ because only $C$ benefits from entering

questions.question: In an entry game, the weak entrant gets $1$ if accommodated, $-2$ if fought and $0$ from staying out. In a mixed perfect Bayesian equilibrium the weak type mixes between In and Out. With what probability must the incumbent accommodate?

An entrant of type $C$ (prior $p$) or $W$ picks Out (payoff $0$) or In; the incumbent sees only In and plays $A$ (accommodate) or $F$ (fight). Payoffs (entrant, incumbent): $C$: $A\,(2,1)$, $F\,(1,-1)$; $W$: $A\,(1,1)$, $F\,(-1,2)$. Let $p=\frac{1}{6}$. In the mixed PBE, $C$ always enters and the incumbent mixes, so $\mu=\frac{1}{3}$. With what probability $q_W$ does $W$ enter?

An entrant of type $C$ (prior $p$) or $W$ picks Out (payoff $0$) or In; the incumbent sees only In and plays $A$ (accommodate) or $F$ (fight). Payoffs (entrant, incumbent): $C$: $A\,(2,1)$, $F\,(1,-1)$; $W$: $A\,(1,1)$, $F\,(-1,2)$. In the mixed PBE for $p=\frac{1}{5}$ the incumbent plays $A$ with probability $\frac{1}{2}$. Why must its belief after In be exactly $\mu=\frac{1}{3}$?
options: Bayes' rule always yields $\frac{1}{3}$ when the weak type mixes
It mixes, so both actions must be optimal, which holds only at $\mu=\frac{1}{3}$
The weak type's indifference requires the belief $\frac{1}{3}$
Off-path beliefs may be chosen freely and $\frac{1}{3}$ is convenient

questions.question: In a Nash equilibrium $\sigma$ of an extensive-form game, every information set is reached with positive probability. If beliefs $\mu$ are derived from $\sigma$ by Bayes' rule, is $(\sigma,\mu)$ a perfect Bayesian equilibrium?
options: Yes: on-path Nash optimality then covers every information set
No: Nash equilibria can still contain non-credible threats
No: PBE also requires each belief to equal the prior
Only if the game has perfect information, with singleton sets

questions.question: An entrant of type $C$ or $W$ gets $0$ from Out and, after In, $1$ if accommodated but $-1$ ($C$) or $-2$ ($W$) if fought. The incumbent's Fight payoff is $-1$ against $C$ and $2$ against $W$; Accommodate gives $1$. Which beliefs $\mu=\mathbb{P}(C\mid\text{In})$ support a PBE where both types stay out?
options: Every $\mu\in[0,1]$
Only $\mu=p$, the prior
Every $\mu\in[0,\frac{1}{3}]$
Every $\mu\in[\frac{1}{3},1]$

questions.question: An entrant of type $C$ (prior $p$) or $W$ picks Out (payoff $0$) or In; the incumbent sees only In and plays $A$ (accommodate) or $F$ (fight). Payoffs (entrant, incumbent): $C$: $A\,(2,1)$, $F\,(1,-1)$; $W$: $A\,(1,1)$, $F\,(-1,2)$. Let $p=\frac{1}{2}$. In a profile, $C$ enters, $W$ stays out and the incumbent plays $A$ after In. Why is this not part of a PBE?
options: Bayes' rule requires $\mu=p=\frac{1}{2}$, not $\mu=1$
With $\mu=1$ the incumbent accommodates, so $W$ would gain $1>0$ by entering
With $\mu=1$ the incumbent should fight, which deters $C$
It is a PBE, since beliefs follow Bayes' rule and accommodating is optimal
